paper_title: HexaShell: A Thin Harness for Exploring the Limits of VLM Agents as Robot Coding Agents

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Agents built on vision language models (VLMs) now compete with learned policies on robot manipulation leaderboards. We ask how far a coding agent can go when it controls a robot instead of a computer, and where it stops. Our system, HexaShell, keeps the harness thin: it only turns the agent's commands into robot motion. The agent drives a robot with two arms through one command line. It sees three RGB cameras and knows their calibration. After each failed attempt, the agent reads the log, finds the cause, and writes or fixes small programs called tools. In this way it keeps what it learns as code, as a coding agent does when it fixes a failing test. The tools may use only what the robot observes. They use triangulation to find where objects are, relative to each other and to the gripper. If two cameras see the same point, the point lies where the two camera rays meet. If a point lies on a known plane, such as the table or the top of a block, it lies where its ray meets that plane. When the head camera is not enough, the robot moves a wrist camera to get a second view. We build the tools on only ten layouts of one seed per task, then freeze them and test them on ten new layouts of the same seed. We use Codex with GPT-6-Astra at medium reasoning effort. On all 42 RoboDojo tasks, HexaShell reaches a success rate of 39.7% and a progress score of 48.0, averaged in the same way as the leaderboard. This is a new state of the art on RoboDojo. The limit is contact, not reasoning: pushing reaches 92.5% and memory tasks 65.0%, but tight insertion only 8.3%. When the agent fails, it usually sees the failure but cannot make the motion work. We open source the tools evolved so far at https://github.com/HexaFuture/HexaShell.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Robot manipulation leaderboards have been led by learned policies. Vision language action models and world action models learn from large sets of demonstrations and output the robots actions directly [4, 7, 35]. Agents built on vision language models have now started to compete. On RoboDojo [14], the model we use reaches 22.5% without tools of its own, choosing gripper targets through fixed harness written by the benchmarks authors [69]. Coding agents suggest another route. In software repository, coding agent reads the code, runs it, reads the error and fixes the code, and the fix stays. Recent work has begun to let coding agents write and revise robot tools and programs [25, 26, 34, 40]. We ask how far coding agent can go when it works on robot in the same way, and where it stops. Our system, HexaShell, keeps the harness thin. The agent gets one command, robo, three RGB images with their calibration, and manual of one page. The harness turns commands into joint motion and does nothing else. What the agent learns is kept as tools, small programs that add commands to robo and may use only what the robot observes. An acting agent tries layout with the current tools. After failure, an optimizer agent of the same model reads the episode as it would read failing test, writes or fixes tool with its unit tests, and the layout is tried again  (Fig. 3)  . Both agents are Codex with GPT-6-Astra at medium reasoning effort. The hard part is turning pixels into positions. In repository, everything the agent works on is text it can read exactly. On robot, the agent sees objects as pixels, but every command needs position in the world, to about centimetre for grasp. Vision language models are known to judge such distances poorly [9, 16]. The standard observation has no depth. monocular depth network can estimate depth from one image, but on RoboDojo scenes Depth Anything V2 [65] is off by median of 41 mm at the head camera and about 100 mm at the wrists, even after we fix its scale with the table. Our tools use triangulation instead. The cameras are calibrated, and the robot knows where its wrists are. point that two cameras see lies where their rays meet, and point on measured plane, such as the table, lies where its ray meets that plane [27]. When one view is not enough, the robot moves wrist camera to get another. This is active perception [3], and on benchmark it has price: the motion uses action steps, and every task has step limit. We build the tools on ten layouts of each task, freeze them, and test them on ten new layouts. On all 42 tasks, HexaShell reaches 39.7% success and progress score of 48.0 on the leaderboards metric, new state of the art on RoboDojo  (Fig. 2)  . It does best where the right action follows from measured geometry, and it stops at contact: tight insertion stays low. The paper makes three contributions. thin harness and short repair loop for robot coding agents. The harness gives an unchanged coding agent one command line to the robot and makes no decisions for it. All that the agent learns is kept as small tools with unit tests, which the next episode loads. After failure, second agent of the same model edits one tool and the same layout runs again. repair round takes median of 6.3 minutes, and no robot data, training or change to the model is needed (Sec. 3). The finding that triangulation locates objects more reliably than depth network, and so lifts what VLM agent achieves on robot. The model picks pixel on the target, and the tool turns it into position. With the same harness, loop and model, on the same layouts, triangulation scores 8.7 points higher than Depth Anything V2; paired by layout, it wins 57 layouts and loses 23 (Tab. 1). Its second views cost at least 3.6% of the executed steps, and on the layouts where the robot moved camera to look, triangulation succeeds 39 times against 22 (Sec. 4.5). map of the current limits of VLM agents in the physical world. Over 420 retest episodes, success follows the contact task needs, not what the agent must read or remember. Pushing reaches 92.5% and memory tasks 65.0%, but tight insertion only 8.3%. On the development layouts, clutter matters little: with 13 to 18 extra objects, HexaShell keeps 95% of its success. How an episode fails also separates gap in perception, where the agent claims success that the checker rejects, from gap in execution, where it runs out of steps (Secs. 4.3 and 5). Seven case studies show the loop at work. Each follows failed attempt through the optimizers diagnosis and fix to the next attempt on the same layout (Sec. 6).

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Language models have written robot code before. Code as Policies [37] emits executable programs over perception and control primitives, ProgPrompt [54] and Inner Monologue [29] plan with language model and feedback, VoxPoser [30] writes value maps for planner, ReKep [31] and MOKA [39] let vision model mark keypoints that code then optimises, RoboCodeX [45] and RoboScript [10] generate manipulation code from images and text, language models write reward functions for policy learning [44, 66], and SayCan [1] grounds language in fixed skill library. In each, the program is produced per instruction and discarded, and people write the primitives. HexaShell inverts this division of labour: the agent writes the primitives, they persist across episodes and are what is optimized, and the per-episode program is short. Concurrent work moves the same way: URAI pairs programming agent that writes motion tools with an execution agent that calls them [26], Gao et al. [25] treat tools, traces and memory as code that physical coding agent revises, CaP-X benchmarks coding agents on manipulation [23], RLE-Bench tests them as robot learning engineers [43], LIBERO-Agent tests general agents that act on the robot directly [18], and MEMENTO evolves code policies with memory of past programs [56]. We measure, on one full benchmark, how far such tools reach and where they stop. Frontier models have also been used as policies without tools of their own. Zhang et al. [69] evaluate GPT-6-Astra on RoboDojo through fixed end-effector harness with no learned policy in the loop, and in case study the model writes piano controller that transfers across tempo but not key geometry. Show-Harness [15], Agent as Policy [32], VIA [28] and World Action Agent [70] drive robots through vision language agent and fixed interface, and line of recent work builds harnesses in which coding agents program, test and improve robot skills [11, 19, 21, 42, 57, 59, 63], sometimes starting from few human demonstrations [34, 40]. We keep the model and benchmark and change one thing, letting the agent write, keep and repair tools (Sec. 5.1). Agents that build their own tools are the closest family. Coding agents that read repository, run the tests and fix the code [12, 33, 62, 64] are the starting point of this paper. Voyager [58] grows skill library of JavaScript functions while playing Minecraft, Toolformer [52] learns when to call existing tools, LATM [8] and CRAFT [67] have language models write and retrieve tools, and self-improving coding agents [41, 47, 68] modify their own scaffolding or programs and keep edits that improve score. Our loop belongs to this family but holds the agents scaffold, prompt and base interface fixed and changes only task tools. We are able to diagnose faults in one round, while ensuring that the tools stay runnable under the official client. Like Reflexion [53] and Eureka [44], the optimizer iterates on code from traces, but acceptance is fresh execution of the same layout rather than self-assessment. Our tools measure 3D positions from RGB images. Monocular depth networks predict depth from one image [5, 60, 61, 65], but their scale must be fixed from outside and their errors are several centimetres on our scenes (Sec. 4.4). Vision language models judge metric distances in an image poorly, and SpatialVLM and SpatialRGPT train them on spatial data to improve this [9, 16]. Multiple view geometry recovers point from two calibrated views [27], and plane sweep tests candidate depths by warping one view into another [17]; both are standard in OpenCV [6]. Active perception moves the sensor to get better view [2, 3]. Our tools combine these ideas and charge each extra view to the robots action budget, which benchmark with step limit makes explicit (Sec. 4.5). 3 sandbox: no simulator, no key Acting agent commands Harness server joint targets RoboDojo simulator validate line IK timing observations dual-arm robot cameras checker coding agent robo observations feedback 1 loaded; same layout again Tool library Optimizer agent passed tools perception execution notes 4 diagnose write or repair check after 10 layouts freeze, retest every layout 2 Episode log on failure 3 commands frames transcript s e e i e e Figure 3. Bottom, between episodes: 2 the episode log keeps the commands, the camera frames and the agents transcript; 3 after failure the optimizer agent diagnoses the episode, 4 writes or fixes tool that must pass delivery check, and 5 the tool is loaded and the same layout is tried again. The baselines we compare against are mostly learned manipulation policies. Vision language action models [4, 7, 35, 48 50, 73], trained on demonstrations collected with low cost hardware [71], are evaluated on suites such as LIBERO [22, 38], RoboCasa [46], RoboTwin [13] and SIMPLER [36], or in autonomous real-world evaluation [72]. RoboDojo [14] adds fixed action budget per task, multi-seed evaluation, and paired clean and cluttered layouts, which let us separate geometric competence from appearance memorisation (Sec. 4.3).

sections.title: 3 HexaShell
sections.content: HexaShell has three parts  (Fig. 3)  : harness that turns commands into motion (Sec. 3.1), tools that measure 3D positions from RGB images (Secs. 3.2 and 3.3), and an evolution loop that turns failures into tools (Sec. 3.4). Four principles shaped them. The harness translates and never decides. Ground truth is isolated by architecture: the container the acting agent runs in holds no simulator, task or scoring code. Success is judged only by the benchmarks own checker, which we do not modify. The manual states interfaces only; strategy lives in tools.

sections.title: 3.1 The harness
sections.content: The acting agent is stock coding agent CLI running in container with no direct network access, no API key and no host directories. It is given one executable, robo, and directory obs/ that is refreshed on request. The directory holds three 640480 RGB images (head and two wrist cameras), each cameras intrinsics and its pose in the world, the two tool centre point (TCP) poses and the joint angles. There is no depth image. The head camera is fixed; each wrist camera pose follows from the TCP pose the robot reports. The manual has about sixty lines. The base commands are move (translate TCP along world axes, at most 0.20 per axis), rotate (about the TCP, at most 90 per axis), point (choose gripper orientation from small set and finger opening axis), gripper, home, wait, obs, status and done. Every command returns JSON record with planning verdict, the reached pose and the remaining budget. Tools appear as additional sub-commands, and their interface.md files are appended to the manual under heading Extra tools for this task. Behind the command line, outbound traffic from the container passes through an egress proxy that adds the model credential and admits only the model endpoint and the harnesss own routes. The server validates each command, interpolates straight Cartesian path at 2 cm spacing, solves inverse kinematics per waypoint with cuRobo [55], and times the joint path with trapezoidal profile under the robots official limits. The timed path is sampled at the benchmarks 25 Hz action rate and sent through the official take_action call. There is no motion planner and no collision model beyond the robot and the table. RoboDojo limits each task by count of action steps (step_lim, from 200 to 1900; 600 for push T, i.e. 24 of robot time). Observations, measurements and model thinking cost nothing, and every executed step costs one. The counter is returned with every response. 4 The same server runs under two executors. direct executor drives the RoboDojo environment in the same process and can reset, replay and log true object poses into field the container never receives. bridge executor wraps the same server as policy for the official evaluation client, which has no reset and no ground truth. The agents interface is the same under both, and every delivered tool must run under the bridge.

sections.title: 3.2 Measuring 3D from RGB images
sections.content: A pixel and the calibration give ray in the world frame. ray alone is not position, so every measurement adds one more constraint. The tools use three kinds, all plain OpenCV geometry [6, 27]. The first constraint is the table. shared tool, table_plane, measures the table height once per episode, the first time it is called, at no step cost. It sweeps candidate heights, warps each camera image into another camera through the plane at that height, and keeps the height where the warped images agree best [17]. The three camera pairs agree to within 1 mm in our runs (0.76460.7656 m). The second constraint is any other plane whose height is known in the episode. The top face of block, the rim of bowl or slot in box lies on horizontal plane; once its height is measured, the ray through pixel on it gives the point. The third constraint is second view. If two cameras see the same point, the two rays nearly meet, and the point between them is the triangulated position. Corresponding pixels come from the acting agent, who picks them in both images, or from template matching, contours and circle fits inside tool. The head camera sees the whole table, but often from too far away or at poor angle, and objects hide each other. The wrist cameras then give the second view, but only after the robot moves them. tool or the agent moves wrist above the target, reads its pose from the TCP, and measures. These moves are robot motion, so they consume steps from the tasks limit. This is the price of measuring without depth, and Sec. 4.5 measures it. The rule for both agents is that every number about an object must be measured in the episode. Object sizes, positions and heights may not come from the benchmarks assets, layouts, configuration or logs.

sections.title: 3.3 Tools
sections.content: A tool is directory with tool.py and interface.md. The Python file declares name, its sub-commands and their arguments, and run(api, command, args) function over an EpisodeAPI. This API offers joint angles, TCP poses, the three RGB images with calibration, and the same motion primitives the base commands use. Tools cannot import the simulator, cannot read object poses, and are loaded only if listed in the tasks enabled_tools.txt. Measurement commands that move nothing are free, so the agent calls them freely. Commands that move an arm, including the ones that move wrist camera to look, return the same planning verdict as base commands and list their stages. shared pool holds two tools, pick and table_plane, which the loop never modifies. Everything else is task specific.

sections.title: 3.4 The evolution loop
sections.content: One command starts run for one task on one GPU. The loop uses the first ten layouts of evaluation seed 0 (for Generalization tasks, five standard and five cluttered, which share tools) and proceeds layout by layout. The acting agent attempts the layout with the current tools. On success, the optimizer agent reads the trajectory and adds short entry to playbook.md on which tools worked and why. On failure, it reads the command log, the camera frames of every command and the current tool code. It writes diagnosis to skill.md and adds or fixes tool. delivery check then verifies that files are complete, tools load, and the interface text names neither the task nor its objects; if the check fails the edit is reverted. The simulator is restarted and the same layout is attempted again, up to five edits per layout. After the tenth layout the optimizer consolidates its notes, the tool set is frozen and tested once more with no optimizer, on the ten development layouts and on ten new layouts (Sec. 4.1). Both agents run GPT-6-Astra at medium reasoning effort. The optimizer writes only under tasks/task/ and cannot touch the harness, the manual or the shared pool. The RGB tools come from one run per task with development budget of 12 hours. Each run started from the tools of our earlier runs with depth, and for 25 tasks the optimizer also read short note on what the checker requires, written from the public task definitions; the acting agent never sees the notes (Sec. D).

sections.title: 4.1 Setup
sections.content: RoboDojo [14] has 42 simulated tasks for dual-arm ARX X5 in Isaac Sim 5.1, grouped into Generalization (12 tasks, each with cluttered variant that adds 13 to 18 distractor objects), Memory, Long-Horizon, Precision and Open. Each task ships three evaluation seeds; seed is set of 30 to 75 scene layouts in which object poses and table materials vary under fixed rules. Success is judged per step by the benchmarks own checker, and the episode ends at the first success. The leaderboards score averages the five task types with equal weight, Generalization being the mean of its standard and cluttered variants; we also report the plain mean over the 54 variants. We compare against the leaderboard as of 14 October 2026, where entries report 50 episodes on each of three seeds. The two highest learned policies are VPP2 (success rate 32.26%, progress score 39.26), world action model, and PhysicalRSI (31.38%, 36.27), VLA directed by language model agent. Thirty entries output actions from learned policy, and we use all of them for the clutter comparison. The same model without tools is GPT-6-Astra choosing bounded gripper targets through the benchmark authors fixed harness, 50 episodes on one seed per task (22.48%, 28.97) [69]. Our main system observes RGB images only and measures with the geometry of Sec. 3.2. Two variants use the same harness and model. In the first, depth network, Depth Anything V2 Base [65], estimates depth inside the server for every image, and its scale is fixed in each frame by the table plane. In the second, the simulator renders depth; this is not part of the standard observation and serves only as reference. Both agents are the unmodified Codex command-line agent with GPT-6-Astra at medium reasoning effort, with one RTX 4090 per run. retest episode takes median of 739 for 26 of robot time, almost all of it model latency, which RoboDojo does not charge. RGB results are frozen retests: one episode on each of ten new layouts, layouts 10 to 19 of seed 0 (standard and cluttered layouts 5 to 9 for Generalization tasks), with the benchmarks checkers. The tools were not built on these layouts. In these retests the agents prompt also holds the tasks description and score table from the benchmarks documentation, as for the benchmark authors agent [69]. It also holds short notes on how the tools behaved in the development runs, and the manual has revised rules for ending an episode. Swap blocks runs with the benchmarks fix of its button reset, and with tools developed again under that fix. The depth network results, and the comparisons in Secs. 4.3 to 4.5 and 5.2, use the ten development layouts, the first ten of seed 0 (five standard and five cluttered for Generalization tasks), with the bare instruction.

sections.title: 4.2 Main results
sections.content: Fig. 2 compares the task types with the leaderboard. On the leaderboards metric HexaShell reaches 39.7% success and progress score of 48.0, above VPP2 (32.3%, 39.3), PhysicalRSI (31.4%, 36.3) and the other learned policies. Over the 54 variants the plain mean is 35.4%, against 30.6% for VPP2, 26.1% for PhysicalRSI and 24.3% for the same model without tools. Per variant, HexaShell is higher than VPP2 on 23, by median of 29 points, and lower on 27, by median of 23  (Fig. 11)  . HexaShell leads where the task is decided by reading the scene and remembering it: Memory (65.0%, against at most 55.6%) and Open (50.0%, against at most 31.0%). Learned policies lead where precise contact decides: VPP2 reaches 35.2% on Precision and 37.0% on Long-Horizon, against our 31.3% and 23.8%. Six variants pass every layout (both variants of push T, the cluttered variant of stack bowls, play tic tac toe, press by number and stack blocks by language), and 19 stay at zero.

The reason lies in what the tools compute: the agent picks pixel on the target, and the tool measures that object and nothing else. sections.title: 4.4 Triangulation versus a depth network
sections.content: Tab. 1 compares three ways for the tools to get 3D. On the same layouts, triangulation scores 8.7 points higher than the depth network on the leaderboards metric. Paired by layout, geometry turns 57 failures of the depth network into successes and loses 23 (exact McNemar test, < 0.001). The largest gains are push (4 to 10 of 10 layouts), imitate sorting sequence (1 to 8) and play Xylophone (0 to 6); six more tasks gain three layouts each. The losses are smaller: pour liquid into cup, pour by language, stack bowls and arrange largest number lose two layouts each. Three of these four put something in or on round container whose rim the tools must measure. Pour balls into vase also uses round container, yet it gains three. The reason is accuracy. Against rendered depth on 300 frames of eight tasks, the depth networks median error on object pixels was 41 mm at the head camera and about 100 mm at the wrists, after we fixed its scale with the table. Three other networks we tried, Depth Pro [5] and two versions of MoGe [60, 61], reduced the head error to 2031 mm but left 2172 mm at the wrists. Grasps and placements need about centimetre. Geometry has no such floor: when its assumption holds, known plane or point visible in two views, the error comes from the calibration and the pixel. Rendered depth is still 10.6 points higher. Most of the gap is in tight insertion, discussed in Sec. 5.

sections.title: 4.6 What the agents built
sections.content: The RGB runs took 769 optimizer rounds (median 17 per task); round after failure took median of 6.3 minutes. The runs left 327 task commands in about 78,000 lines of Python, counting the modules they import (Tab. 6). In the retests on the development layouts, 42 commands were called with second camera, 998 times in 25 tasks. The measurements fall into few patterns: plane height from camera pair, point on measured plane, triangulated point, patch or contour, and rim fitted in two views. The model picks the pixel and the code measures the world. This split keeps the tools easy to check, and, as Sec. 5 shows, it also sets their limits. Sec. follows push through its development.

sections.title: 5 Where the boundary lies
sections.content: The averages hide sharp split: 18 variants are at or above 50% and 19 are at 0%. To find what separates them we use the retests of the RGB tools.

sections.title: 5.1 A capability map
sections.content: We label every task twice (Tab. 5). The physical label names the contact that success requires: rigid pick, place or stack with centimetre tolerance (R); pushing, sliding or pressing (Pu); insertion or placement with millimetre or few-degree tolerance (In); articulated objects or held tool used through several contacts (Ar); deformable, fluid or granular material (Df); and objects that move on their own (Mv). The decision label names what must be decided beyond geometry: nothing (G), reading symbols, following language or recognising categories (S), or remembering an earlier state (M). Each task has one of each. The physical interaction decides (Tab. 3). Pushing reaches 92.5% and rigid manipulation 50.0%; moving objects reach 40.0% and deformable material 33.3%, articulated objects 7.5%, and tight insertion 8.3%, with 7 of its 12 variants at 8 zero. The decision load matters less, except for memory (65.0%). VPP2 has the opposite profile: it is weaker on pushing (24.7%) and rigid manipulation (30.0%), and stronger on insertion (28.1%), deformable material (49.4%) and articulated objects (21.6%). What the tools add is the gap to the column without tools. They add most where the right action can be computed from measured geometry: pushing gains 33 points, rigid manipulation 13 and memory 26. Articulated objects gain little, mostly from play Xylophone (6 of 10 layouts); these are the first articulated successes in any of our runs. On cloth the tools still do worse than an agent that corrects step by step: fold clothes reaches 50% against 72% without tools. tool fixes one interpretation and one motion planned in advance; an agent acting step by step can still notice and correct. Tight insertion and pouring are where measuring without depth costs most. With rendered depth, the tools reach 30.1% on insertion, led by insert key (80%) and play stacking toy (73%), while the RGB tools reach 8.3%. Pouring falls as far: pour liquid into cup and pour by language drop from 5995% to 010%. An insertion needs the hole and the part in the same frame to few millimetres. At the head camera one pixel covers 23 mm on the table, and the wrist views that would resolve the hole must be made while the gripper holds the part.

sections.title: 5.2 How episodes fail
sections.content: Of the 420 retest episodes on the development layouts, 268 failed. Five of them ended early on tool error; of the other 263, 57% exhausted the budget, 30% ended with the agent declaring completion and the checker disagreeing, 13% ended with the agent giving up while quarter or more of the budget remained, and two were stopped by the checker for rule violation. The mix differs by class (Tab. 3), and the difference is diagnostic. On deformable material, articulated objects and rigid tasks, 6077% of the failures exhaust the budget: the agent sees that the result is wrong and retries until the steps run out, so it knows it has failed and cannot make the motion work. On memory tasks half of the failures are declared successes: the agent believes it has reproduced the earlier state, and the checker disagrees. This fits the known weakness of vision language models at fine visual detail [24, 51] and at judging success [20]. Moving objects often show third signature: the agent gives up once the object it was waiting for has passed. declared failure therefore points to gap in perception or in the tasks specification, an exhausted one to gap in execution.

sections.title: 5.3 Missing information or missing capability?
sections.content: In an earlier run with rendered depth, short notes on what the checker requires lifted three tasks from 040% to 95100% (Tab. 7). The notes stayed available in the RGB runs. On the development layouts, press by number keeps 9 of 10 layouts and pour balls into vase 7, but pour liquid into cup falls to 1, while spending fifth of its steps on viewing. Knowing what the checker wants is necessary but not enough: the tool must also measure the cup, and without depth it is still too weak.

sections.title: 6 Case studies: from a failed attempt to a working tool
sections.content: The results above come from frozen tools. This section shows how the tools got there. Each case follows one layout through one turn of the loop of Sec. 3.4: an attempt that fails, the optimizer round that follows, and the next attempt on the same layout with the edited tool.

sections.title: 6.1 What an optimizer round looks like
sections.content: The RGB runs took 769 optimizer rounds. Of these, 530 followed failure, 195 followed success and recorded what had worked, and 42 closed run. round after failure took median of 6.3 minutes, and 90% of them took less than 11. In that time the optimizer ran median of 16 shell commands. It reads its role and the focus file of the round, the failure table, the command log of the failed episode, the acting agents transcript and the code of the enabled tools. It then edits tool, writes or updates unit tests and runs them; 92% of these rounds ran the tasks tests. The median edit added 118 lines and removed 6, tests and notes included. round read median of 0.75 million input tokens, most of them cached, and wrote 5.7 thousand. Over all rounds the optimizer read 487 million input tokens and wrote 3.8 million. 9 In 27 tasks layout failed and then passed on the next attempt after an edit, 67 times in all. success after an edit can also come from different choice by the acting agent or different turn of the scene. For each candidate we checked in the log of the successful attempt that the edited code ran and that it addressed what had failed, and for two cases we ran the old and the new code on the stored images. Tab. 4 lists the seven cases we kept, at least one for each physical class of Tab. 3. In five of them the optimizer looked at no image: the command log, the tools feedback and the code were enough. In fold clothes it ran its code on stored test images, and only in swap did it analyse frame of the failed episode. Table 4. Seven turns of the loop. Each row is one layout: the attempts that failed on it before the success (Fails), what the optimizer found after the last failure, what it changed, the size of the edit in lines added and removed (tests included) and the length of the round in minutes, the action steps of the next attempt, which succeeded, and the frozen retest of the same layout, with the tasks retest over its ten development layouts.

sections.title: 6.2 Push T: a height check that compared unequal pixels
sections.content: In push the robot pushes block onto pad. The block must end within 7 mm and 7 degrees of the pad, with both arms at home. The tools project the blocks outline from the head camera onto plane at the blocks top, and stereo command measures the height of that plane from two cameras. On layout 2 in round 4 the height command refused all ten requests that reached its area check: it found the blocks area in the two views too different. The agent fell back to the table height, 0.765 m, while the top of the block is at 0.780 m. The 15 mm error shifted the projected outline by 10 mm. The first transfer left the block 3.2 mm from the pad, inside the limit, but the release check used the same wrong height and reported 12.5 mm. The agent corrected three times and ended 13.6 mm off  (Fig. 4)  . The optimizer found the cause in the code, from the tools error messages: The stereo code estimates area by counting occupied grid cells; distant camera can therefore report smaller area than close camera for the same surface. The coarse pixels of the head camera fill only about quarter of the 1 mm cells that the close wrist camera fills. The 10 Figure 4. Push T, layout 2: height that the tool refused. Left wrist camera. (a) and (c) show almost the same placement; only the measured height of the blocks top differs. optimizer replaced the count with the sum of each pixels footprint on the plane. Its new test, with two cameras of different resolution, failed before the fix and passed after, and all 73 tests passed. In round 5 the first height request returned 0.780 m, and the agent used it for every later step. The release check reported 1.6 mm, the true error was 3.0 mm, and the episode succeeded at step 354 of 600. On the stored images of that request the old code finds the same height but rejects it, with an area ratio of 0.27 against lower bound of 0.85. With frozen tools layout 2 passed again in 251 steps, and push passed all ten development layouts, standard and cluttered. Sec. follows the whole push run.

sections.title: 6.3 Swap T: a colour mask that mixed two faces
sections.content: In swap the robot exchanges two blocks. Each block must end within 2 cm of the others start and within 3 degrees of its heading. On layout 0, round 1 failed when recovery turned block twice, and the optimizer enabled measuring tool, surface_pair, which fits the outlines of both blocks and returns the turn between them. In round 2 the acting agent called surface_pair seven times, and each call failed to measure the block height. It then typed height of 0.78 m, and the tool returned turn of 130.6 degrees with an outline fit error of 2.6 mm. Both blocks ended within 5 mm of their targets, and the check failed on their headings  (Fig. 5)  . Figure 5. Swap T, layout 0: two faces of one colour. (a, c) left wrist camera; (b, d) head camera, cropped. The optimizer turned to the angle. It clustered the colours of the last head frame and found that each block splits into bright top face and darker side face of the same hue: Im investigating whether the color masks mixed top and side faces, which would distort both height and rotation estimates. It also found that the tool matched one fixed colour across the cameras, while each camera sees the blocks under different light. It built synthetic scene with both effects, and the old tool failed on it with the episodes error. It changed 28 lines of surface_pair to match colours by hue and to keep only the bright top face in each view. All 80 tests passed. In round 3 surface_pair measured the height itself, 0.781 m, and returned turn of 126.2 degrees with an outline fit error of 0.4 mm. The swap passed at step 285 of 400. Each block of round 2 had ended about 3 degrees from where it ended 11 in round 3. With frozen tools layout 0 passed again in 275 steps, with measured turn of 126.3 degrees, and the task passed all ten development layouts.

sections.title: 6.4 Play Xylophone: a second view of a held tool
sections.content: In play Xylophone the robot picks up mallet and strikes the eight keys from left to right. The checker counts key when the mallet head is inside its box, 1.0 to 3.6 cm above it, and lifted at least 2.5 cm before the next key. The tasks note states these numbers, and the tools default heights follow them. Layout 1 failed four times, each time for different reason: plans rejected for clearance, ball outline that was not round, grasp on the stand instead of the mallet, and in round 9 the position of the held mallet. In round 9 the acting agent lifted the mallet and measured its head with rgb_sphere from the head camera alone, using the radius of the head to set the range. The estimate was 22.9 mm from the true centre. Two sequence plans failed the reach check, so the agent moved all eight targets 5 to 8 cm toward the near ends of the keys. The third plan ran all eight strikes, and the checker counted none  (Fig. 6)  . Figure 6. Play Xylophone, layout 1: one view against two. (a) head camera, cropped; (bd) right wrist camera. The optimizer traced the miss to the estimate of the held mallet head from one camera, and changed rgb_sphere. Given one pixel on the ball, the tool now finds the matching ball in another current camera and triangulates the centre. The radius only filters the candidates, and without clear match the tool fails instead of guessing. In its new synthetic test the old method erred by 22.7 mm and the new one by less than 2 mm. All 35 tests passed. In round 10 the first call failed, because the ball was cut off at the border of the wrist view. The agent moved both arms until the right wrist camera saw the whole head. The tool matched the two views and put the centre 2.7 mm from the true one, with 0.7 mm between the two rays. The sequence ran at the measured key centres on its first plan, and the task succeeded at step 377 of 500. In the frozen retest layout 1 passed again, this time with strikes made by base moves, and the task passed 6 of its 10 development layouts. The depth network version passed none.

sections.title: 6.5 Match and pick from conveyor: a schedule the arm could not meet
sections.content: In match and pick from conveyor the robot remembers the first object on moving belt and picks the matching object when it comes back. On layout 4 in round 9 the tools located the green toy to within 3 to 11 mm. Twice the agent asked the tool timed_pick for short schedule, with the descent due 0.80 after the call. Turning and moving the arm took 1.56 s, so both times the tool aborted before it went down, and the open fingers waited above the passing toy. manual grasp then closed 67 mm behind it  (Fig. 7)  . The optimizer saw that vision was fine and the schedules were impossible: The trace also shows two approaches that consumed motion time before reporting missed deadline, plus completed pick that did not retain the object. It found server call that estimates the cost of motion without moving the arm, and added check to timed_pick. Before moving, the tool now estimates each stage. If the schedule is too short, it moves the closing time later and the meeting point further down the belt. All 20 tests passed. In round 10 the agent again asked for short pick, closing at 1.5 s. Getting into place took 1.68 s, so the old tool would have aborted again. The new check moved the closing time to 2.16 and the meeting point 64 mm further along the belt. The arm reached the toy as its approach ended, closed on it and lifted it, and the task succeeded at step 587 of 700. In the frozen retest layout 4 passed in 460 steps, and the task passed 7 of its 10 development layouts. 12 Figure 7. Match and pick from conveyor, layout 4: time, not position. (a, c) right wrist camera; (b) head camera, cropped. (c) is the last frame of the video, since the episode ended during the lift.

sections.title: 6.6 Play tic tac toe: a route that saves steps
sections.content: In play tic tac toe the robot plays first and fills the board with scripted opponent: five rings from the robot, four crosses from the opponents arm, within 1100 action steps. On layout 0 in round 3 the first four rings landed within 6 mm of their cells, but these placements used 1016 steps. Waiting for the opponent took 520 of them. Before each transfer the tool turned the empty gripper at the home pose, at 16 to 22 steps time. The first entry also stopped 8.1 mm short of its depth, over the 8 mm limit, and cost 56 steps to redo. The route for the last ring needed 146 steps when 84 were left, and the agent sent both arms home with one cell empty  (Fig. 8)  . Figure 8. Play tic tac toe, layout 0: the step budget. (a, b) head camera, cropped, before the last ring; (c) right wrist camera, last frame of the video. The optimizer read the step count of every transfer from the log. It kept the waits, which the game requires, and went after the turns: The transfer tool rotates the empty gripper at home before moving above the source. Ill check whether combining those two motions can save enough steps while preserving vertical contact moves and clearance. The transfer now also plans route that turns the gripper while it moves above the ring, keeps the fingertips above the travel height during the turn, and takes the cheaper reachable route. The optimizer added eight tests, and all 192 passed. In round 4 all five transfers took the combined route. The first placement fell from 152 to 128 steps, and the next three from 344 to 312. The first entry stopped inside the depth limit this time, and the cell order left nearer cell for the last ring. Before the last ring 140 steps remained, and its route needed 129. The board filled at step 1028 of 1100. In the frozen retest layout 0 passed at step 1035, and the task passed 9 of its 10 development layouts.

sections.title: 6.7 Fold clothes: a grasp point on the edge
sections.content: In fold clothes the robot folds both sleeves of shirt across the body and then makes last fold. The cluttered variant places other objects around it. On layout 1 in round 13 the landmark tool cloth_view placed the grasp point of the left 13 sleeve 1.5 mm from the cloth edge, and the gripper pinched only the edge of the cuff. The left sleeve stayed out. The acting agent saw this, grasped the sleeve again at its middle and left it bunched on its own side. The last fold scored nothing, and the episode ended at step 453 of 500  (Fig. 9)  . Figure 9. Fold clothes, cluttered layout 1: where to grasp sleeve. Head camera, cropped, after the sleeve folds (a, c) and after the repair grasp of round 13 (b) and the crossed sleeves of round 14 (d). The optimizer read the transcript and the tools feedback, then ran the grasp point code on four stored test images with their calibration and measured each points distance to the cloth edge: On four archived RGB fixtures, lateral contacts sit only 0.97.4 mm from an edge despite the nominal 25 mm inset. The cause was check that accepted point when one pixel of it fell on the cloth, and returned an unchecked point when it found none. The optimizer replaced it with test on the table plane that requires 12 mm of cloth on every side of the point, searched on 2 mm grid up to 6 cm inward. All 37 tests passed. Between rounds 13 and 14 only cloth_view changed. In round 14 it returned points 12.3 and 12.1 mm inside the edge; on the same frame the old code returns points 1.6 and 5.4 mm from it. The left sleeve crossed the body in one move, no repair was needed, and the shirt was folded at step 344 of 500. In the frozen retest this layout failed with progress of 20%, and the task passed 6 of its 10 development layouts.

sections.title: 6.8 Insert tubes: an early stop in the hardest class
sections.content: In insert tubes the robot places three tubes upright in the holes of rack. Insertion is the class where the RGB tools do worst (Sec. 5.1), and layout 4 failed in rounds 16, 17 and 18. In round 18 the agent grasped the first tube and called rigid_place. The arm lifted the tube and stopped: no path to the rack was clear. After the lift, stereo found nothing near the path, so the tool fell back on single camera rays and marked 28,935 voxels along them as obstacles, although their depth was never measured. Both alternative paths failed inverse kinematics, and the tool gave up, although the original path had passed its check before the lift. Recovery by hand cost 108 of the 500 steps. later tube was released after 5.7 mm lowering error and fell across the rack, and the agent quit at step 449  (Fig. 10)  . Figure 10. Insert tubes, layout 4: stop after the lift. (a, b, d) head camera, cropped; (c) left wrist camera. The optimizer read the tools feedback and the command log: The clearance fallback treated 28,935 voxels along monocular rays as hard constraint, although their depths were unverified. It rejected both proposed yaw paths and stranded the grasp. It kept those rays as preference and added one more check: when the preferred paths are rejected, the tool rechecks the original remaining path from the joints it has reached and goes on if that path is reachable. Obstacles 14 seen in two views still block the move. All 183 tests passed. The optimizer noted that the change does not explain the sideways release. In round 19 the same situation came up, with 27,626 ray voxels and two rejected paths. The recheck passed, and the first tube reached its hole 1.5 mm from the measured centre. Lowering stopped early, and the agent opened the gripper and let the tube drop in. The first tube took 64 steps instead of 108, the other two needed moves by hand, and the episode succeeded at step 398 of 500. In the frozen retest layout 4 passed in 411 steps without needing the recheck, and the task passed 3 of its 10 development layouts. The other seven ended with the agent quitting or at the step limit.

sections.title: 6.9 What the cases show
sections.content: The optimizer works like programmer reading bug report. Its evidence is mostly numbers: the step count of each command, the reason tool gave for refusing. Its edits are small and local. Each changes one tool, comes with new tests, and leaves the strategy to the acting agent. Three of the seven fix measurement (push T, swap T, play Xylophone), two fix timing (the conveyor schedule and the tic tac toe route), one fixes where to grasp (fold clothes) and one fixes when tool gives up (insert tubes). In insert tubes the fix removed one obstacle, and the tube still went in by drop. This matches the boundary of Sec. 5: round of the loop can repair what the agent measures and plans, but not the contact that tight insertion needs.

sections.title: 7 Conclusion
sections.content: HexaShell gives an unchanged coding agent one command line to robot and keeps what the agent learns as small tools, repaired after each failure in round of few minutes. With triangulation from calibrated RGB cameras, the tools locate objects more reliably than depth network, and on ten new layouts of all 42 RoboDojo tasks the agent reaches 39.7% success and progress score of 48.0. The limit is contact, not reasoning: pushing and memory tasks succeed most of the time, but tight insertion stays low, and most failed episodes run out of steps while the agent sees that the motion is not working. Closing this gap is the next step: tools that keep measuring while the gripper holds the part and correct the motion during contact, instead of planning it in advance.

sections.title: B Tools of the RGB runs
sections.content: Tab. 6 lists, for every task, the commands of the frozen RGB tools, the code behind them, the optimizer rounds it took and the share of executed steps spent on viewing moves (Sec. 4.5). Example development log: push The RGB run of push took 13 optimizer rounds and four hours over its ten development layouts. It started from tool of an earlier run, planar_contact, which registered the block against its target outline in the head depth image and carried it there. Without depth this registration failed, but the acting agent passed layouts 0 and 1 anyway, measuring heights by hand with base commands and the shared table tool. Layout 2 failed twice. In round 3 the optimizer rewrote the registration, the height measurement, the handover between the arms and the release check to use RGB silhouettes and calibrated rays. In round 4 it fixed the check that compares the blocks area in two views, which rejected matching views because the two cameras have different pixel scales. From then on every layout passed at the first attempt, standard and cluttered. Rounds 5 to 12 only added notes to the playbook, and round 13 consolidated them. The frozen retest passed all ten layouts, using 245 to 570 of the 600 steps, against 4 of 10 for the depth network version. 20 Figure 12. Progress score per task variant on the development layouts, HexaShell with triangulation against (a) the depth network version and (b) the same model without tools. Points above the diagonal favour triangulation. Colour and shape give the physical class (Sec. 5.1): rigid and push (R, Pu), insertion (In), and articulated, deformable or moving (Ar, Df, Mv). sections.title: D The earlier depth runs and the audit
sections.content: The RGB tools grew out of two earlier lines. The first used rendered depth. Its fully automatic first round, on all 42 tasks, reached 38.0% on the leaderboards metric. second round gave the optimizer short notes on what the checker requires for the tasks where it lagged most (Tab. 7), and team member rebuilt the tool of build tower by hand. Its current tools reach 48.8% (Tab. 1). The second line kept these tools but replaced rendered depth with Depth Anything V2 Base [65] inside the server. We developed 22 tasks again for up to 24 hours each, kept the new tools of ten of them, and the line reached 29.6%. The RGB runs started from the tools of the second line. The notes of the first line stayed in the task directories and were given to the optimizer in every round. By the time of the RGB runs, 25 tasks had such note, written by us from the public task definitions. They state the success conditions and, for some tasks, object sizes or target positions from these definitions. The acting agent never sees them. Nine tasks also started from RGB tools written by colleague with another coding agent. After the RGB runs we audited every enabled tool for numbers that could come from the benchmarks assets, layouts or configuration, by comparing every literal in the tools with the sizes and positions in the task definitions and in the logs. The tools of seven tasks held fixed object geometry: part sizes and templates of fixed scene parts, mostly in the colleagues tools. These tasks are store tools in toolbox, pick from conveyor by image, insert key, hang mugs, fill pen holder, fill egg holder and deposit coin. With the fixed geometry they had passed 3 of their 70 retest layouts. We replaced each constant with measurement made in the episode, retested the seven tasks without further development, and report only these retests; all are 0/10.

sections.title: E Interface given to the acting agent
sections.content: The acting agents manual is one Markdown file, the same for every task; the interface.md of each enabled task tool is appended to it under the heading Extra tools for this task. It contains, in this order: World frame. One right-handed frame for both arms and all cameras, in metres, degrees and seconds; origin on the floor between the arm bases, +x to the robots right, +y away from it, +z up; nominal table top at z=0.74 (the shared table_plane tool measures the real height, about 0.765); arm bases at x= 0.30, y= 0.45; how the frame appears in the head image, with top-view drawing. Gripper. The TCP is the midpoint between the fingertips; the tool frames is the approach direction and the opening axis; gripper value 1 is fully open (8.8 cm), 0 closed, and only the commanded value is reported. reach envelope: pointing straight down the TCP reaches about y=0.00 at table height, pointing down45 about y=0.15. 21 Base commands. obs and status (free); move (translate the TCP along world axes, at most 0.20 per axis), rotate (about the TCP in the world or tool frame, at most 90 per axis), point (down, forward or down45, with required opening axis), gripper, home, wait (at most 5 s), each costing simulation time; done, which ends the episode. Limits. 60 commands per episode; simulation time limited per task; the simulation only runs while command runs; thinking costs no simulation time. Feedback. One JSON object per command: the request, clipping and workspace flags, plan_ok with failure reason (ik_unreachable, self_collision, table_collision, workspace_limit), the reached pose and its error, settled, the gripper value, the time used and left, the commands left, and episode_over; exit codes for argument errors, failed commands, finished episode and client time-outs. Motion planning knows the arm and the table, not the objects. Observations. Head and two wrist RGB images (640480) and state.json with both TCP poses, joint angles, gripper values, and each cameras intrinsics and camera-to-world extrinsics, followed by the formulas that project world point to pixel and turn pixel into ray. There is no depth; the manual names the shared table_plane tool and the two ways to fix point on ray, measured plane or second view. Rules. When the task is finished, home both arms and then call done; call done only when sure; read failed commands output before deciding; object positions are not given and must be worked out from the images and the calibration.

sections.title: F Optimizer role description
sections.content: The optimizer receives 62-line role description and, each round, focus.md that selects one of three modes. In failure mode it reads the failure category, every command with its target, the reached pose, the acting agents trajectory and the head-camera frames; decides which perception tool, execution tool or repair would have prevented the failure, or that the failure was bad luck and nothing should change; implements it under tasks/task/tools/; enables it; and appends dated entry to skill.md. In success mode it appends at most 15 lines to playbook.md and changes no tool unless one misbehaved. In final mode it rewrites playbook.md and skill.md (under 60 lines each) and every interface.md (under 12 lines). Six rules apply throughout: tool may use only the EpisodeAPI (joint angles, TCP poses, motion primitives, the latest observation, the callers arguments) and must never read simulator state or hard-code layout-specific numbers; positions come from OpenCV geometry on the RGB images and the calibration, and no size, height or position of an object may come from the benchmarks assets, layouts, configuration or logs; an interface.md describes the interface only and may not name the task or its objects, which the delivery check enforces with list of banned words; the shared pool is read-only; tools validate their arguments, return planning verdict like the base commands and never raise; and the optimizer runs no evaluations. Each round ends with 310 line proposal.md.
